blocks.text: The life of living organisms is a reflection of what is going on in their bodies. The sum of all the chemical activities occurring in living organisms, metabolism, is regulated by enzymes.

blocks.title: Enzyme
blocks.text: Enzymes are specific proteins that speed up specific chemical reactions by lowering the required activation energy, but are unaltered themselves in the process. Enzymes are also known as biocatalysts.

The rates of enzyme-catalysed reactions may be 10 to the power 3 to 10 to the power 8 times greater than the rates of the corresponding uncatalysed reactions. Not all cells have the same set of enzymes: the chemical reactions going on in red blood cells are very different from those in a nerve cell, because the two contain different sets of enzymes.

blocks.title: Without enzymes, no life
blocks.text: A reaction that is catalysed by an enzyme and completed in 30 minutes would take one year to complete without the enzyme. Without enzymes there would have been no life at all.
Where enzymes are made and where they work

All enzymes are synthesised inside cells by ribosomes. After synthesis they either stay and work inside the cell or are secreted out to work at other sites. Inside the cell many enzymes are dissolved in the cytoplasm, for example the enzymes of glycolysis. Many are tightly bound to the membranes of certain organelles, for example the enzymes of the Calvin cycle and the Krebs cycle. Some enzymes are an integral part of ribosomes, for example the enzymes of protein synthesis.

blocks.title: An enzyme in the wrong place
blocks.text: Some enzymes could prove harmful if they became active in the wrong place. Pepsin is a protein-digesting enzyme that could destroy the protein structures inside the cells where it is synthesised. That is why it is produced in an inactive form (pepsinogen) and secreted out of the cells; when it reaches its target site of action it is activated to pepsin.
The active site of an enzyme

Enzymes are three-dimensional globular proteins, made of polypeptide chains coiled upon themselves. On the surface of the globular enzyme molecule there is a small cleft or depression consisting of only a few amino acids. This is the active site, the location at which catalysis occurs. The shape of the active site of each enzyme is very specific, so only a certain substrate molecule can fit into it; it is three-dimensional and bears a specific charge.

The active site has two distinct regions, the binding site and the catalytic site. The substrate molecule fits into the binding site by weak chemical forces such as hydrogen bonds. The catalytic site catalyses the reaction, and the substrate is transformed into products.

blocks.caption: The active site of an enzyme, and a cofactor changing its shape (original diagram after Figure 5.1).
blocks.long_description: The enzyme is a globular protein of coiled polypeptide chains. Its active site is a small, three-dimensional cleft of a few amino acids with a specific charge. The binding site holds the substrate by weak bonds such as hydrogen bonds; the catalytic site stresses the substrate's bonds and turns it into products. Some enzymes have a non-functional active site until a cofactor such as a metal ion attaches, which changes the enzyme's shape so the substrate can bind.
